briefing.opening: Good morning/afternoon. We will now commence the climate briefing for October 22, 2026.

sections.title: 🔴 Escalating Climate Crisis Warnings and Collapsing Targets
sections.content: News released today vividly illustrates the escalating severity of the climate crisis. Efforts to prevent a 1.5-degree Celsius rise in global temperature have failed. Instead, there is a growing recognition that a 50% reduction in greenhouse gas emissions over the next decade is necessary to defend against a 1.7-degree Celsius increase [3, 12]. UN reports anticipate that climate change will surpass previous predictions, warning that global climate action is 'dangerously insufficient' [150, 153, 154, 157]. Notably, the increase in U.S. greenhouse gas emissions accounts for 70% of the global increase, drawing criticism for exacerbating climate change risks and raising concerns that this could lead to a 2.8°C rise in global temperature [14, 155]. Climate change is already altering the physical form of our planet, with a grim forecast that nearly all shallow-water coral reefs worldwide will face ecosystem collapse by 2075 [138, 143, 160].

sections.title: ⚠️ Specific Impacts of Climate Change and Adaptation Efforts
sections.content: The impacts of climate change are manifesting concretely in our daily lives and across natural ecosystems. Domestically, the risks associated with winter leisure activities have increased, leading to expanded safety standards for outdoor ice. Warnings of a climate crisis from glaciers, such as Himalayan floods and heatwaves on the Korean Peninsula, continue [2, 16]. The importance of utilizing ocean records to understand climate change is being emphasized, with calls for data continuity despite satellite replacements. Attribution studies on heatwaves are underway to estimate the probabilistic and temperature-related impacts of climate change on extreme heat events [1, 6, 7]. Internationally, billions of dollars in damage from hail are being exacerbated by climate change, and physical damages such as the 'Armageddon' of European beaches and North County coastline erosion are being reported [136, 142, 144]. Amidst these crises, apple farmers in Mungyeong are seeking future agricultural solutions, and in Europe, efforts to adapt to climate change by utilizing sorghum are also being observed [10, 141].

sections.title: 🌱 Expansion of Domestic Carbon Neutrality Practices and Increased Social Participation
sections.content: Domestically, various stakeholders are actively pursuing efforts to achieve carbon neutrality. Gwangmyeong City is accelerating public-private cooperative carbon neutrality by signing agreements with businesses and waste management associations and expanding '1.5℃ Climate Volunteer' activities [17, 23, 25, 49, 64], and various local governments, including Namyangju and Gyeongsan City, are establishing greenhouse gas reduction hubs through the opening of carbon neutrality support centers and mobile environmental education programs [21, 24, 34, 66, 70]. In Jeonju City, over 26,000 citizens have participated in carbon neutrality education, spreading a culture of practical action [27, 30, 31, 44, 51, 69], and KEPCO KDN is raising awareness among future generations by conducting carbon neutrality education for elementary school students [11]. Furthermore, carbon neutrality is emerging as a core element of corporate competitiveness, with companies that disclose greenhouse gas reduction plans able to secure funding at lower interest rates [4, 13].

sections.title: 🇰🇷 Accelerating Renewable Energy Transition and Current Challenges
sections.content: The transition to renewable energy is accelerating, reshaping South Korea's power landscape. According to Korea Power Exchange data, renewable energy installed capacity has surpassed that of coal-fired power for the first time ever, emerging as a primary power source [84, 92, 94, 111, 116]. The government plans to elevate 'Renewable Energy Day' to its first official commemorative day and hold a formal ceremony [82]. Various local governments, including Gyeongnam, Yeongcheon, and Gwangju, are securing Nakdong River and Han River basin funds to promote special support projects for renewable energy [77, 81, 83, 95, 101, 115, 118, 119, 122, 132], and businesses across the industry are busy seeking profit models, including jointly targeting AI data centers and new renewable energy markets, and developing overseas transmission networks and renewable energy projects [71, 74, 76, 104, 106, 110, 113, 128, 135]. However, many challenges remain, such as calls to scrap indiscriminate renewable energy development policies, the reality that financial support for fossil fuels is 2.2 times that for renewable energy, and the issue of inadequate transmission of electricity generated by renewable energy facilities, despite their capacity surpassing coal [75, 93, 107, 114].

briefing.closing: Today's briefing highlights the severity of the climate crisis, alongside the coexistence of diverse global and domestic response efforts. Despite the failure to meet targets, the commitment to renewable energy transition and carbon neutrality continues. However, stronger, more consistent policies and tangible transformations are urgently needed. This concludes today's climate briefing.
